title: Intel Stock Has Given Back About 60% Since June. Is It a Buy Now?

Intel Stock Has Given Back About 60% Since June. Is It a Buy Now?
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 3:57 PM CST 5 min read
INTC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock closed at a record of about $141 on June 22. As I write, it trades near $56, about 60% lower.

The latest drop was on Monday, Nov. 16, when shares fell 6% or more by late morning.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Chip stocks broadly slid that day. The Commerce Department had just said it would require licenses to export advanced chips to five countries, including Malaysia and Singapore.

But the bigger issue for Intel stock has been the profit forecast the company gave on Oct. 29. And even after the slide, shares are up around 50% in 2026.

I passed on the stock just last week, when it was near $62. Has the price finally dropped far enough to buy?

Image source: Intel.

A sharp profit reset

Intel's adjusted earnings grew steadily during the first nine months of 2026. Non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share came in at $0.29 in the first quarter, $0.42 in the second, and $0.52 in the third. The adjusted gross margin improved from 41% in Q1 to 41.8% in Q2 and 44.1% in Q3. And revenue from the data center and AI segment climbed 78% year over year to $7.3 billion in Q3, picking up from 59% growth in Q2 and 22% in Q1.

The fourth-quarter outlook undoes much of this progress. Intel sees revenue of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion, a 38% adjusted gross margin, and $0.25 of adjusted earnings per share. Some of that comes from an October accident that stopped production at Intel's plant in Israel, which the company expects to drag on profits in Q4 and into mid-2027.

In other words, quarterly profit is set to fall by more than half from one quarter to the next.

PCs are the biggest reason. Management blamed higher memory prices and tight IT budgets, and it expects industrywide PC unit sales to fall around 12% in 2026. For 2027, Intel is planning for another slide of about 10%, with the bigger drops in the first half.

True, the server side's still growing fast. But Intel's PC-focused client segment took in $8.1 billion in Q3 (more than data center and AI did), so a deep PC slump can lower the whole company's profits.

The stock still assumes a quick rebound

Add the fourth-quarter guidance to Intel's first three quarters, and 2026 adjusted earnings per share would total around $1.48. It'd be more than triple the $0.42 Intel earned in 2025.

title: Intel shareholders sue CEO, CFO after stock rout
detail:
Intel shareholders sue CEO, CFO after stock rout
Intel Executive Vice President Alex Katouzian holds up a new chip on stage during a keynote event during COMPUTEX on June 02, 2026 in Taipei, Taiwan · CFO Dive · Cheng Chia Huang via Getty Images
Grace Noto
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 3:01 PM CST 4 min read
INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

This story was originally published on CFO Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily CFO Dive newsletter.

Intel shareholders filed a proposed class action suit against the semiconductor maker, its CEO and CFO Friday alleging they had failed to properly disclose the full impact of weakening PC demand on company results.

Filed on behalf of the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System by Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd, a shareholder rights and securities fraud litigation firm, the suit claims that leadership, including Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner, failed to disclose adverse facts related to its key PC segment, including an inventory glut and supply chain challenges.

The executives failed to disclose that a "slowdown in PC end market sales was having a materially greater negative impact to Intel's third quarter 2026 CCPG results than defendants had disclosed to investors," the complaint filed in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, San Jose Division reads.

CCPG refers to Intel's "client computing and physical AI group," a segment which includes PC sales and has historically been its best-performing area, according to the Nov. 13 suit. However, growing demand for AI data centers has led to chip shortages which have impacted the segment in recent quarters, bumping up component prices and slowing demand. 

The relationship between data center and PC demand represents a tricky push-pull for the Santa Clara, California-based Intel, which faces both growing demand for the CPU chips needed inside both AI data centers and consumer personal devices. The company, which is backed by investors including Nvidia — a fellow AI darling facing its own unfolding crisis — and the U.S. government, has moved to position itself as a key player in the AI boom, with both Tan and Zinsner pointing to key growth opportunities represented by expanding demand for AI data centers.

Despite strong data center demand signals for its most recent quarter, however, those tailwinds were more than offset by subsequent weakness in its PC segment that sent shares tumbling and spiked investor concerns. Weaker-than-anticipated CCPG revenue in Q3, combined with a weak Q4 forecast, sent Intel shares tumbling by as much as 29% the following Friday, according to reports at the time.

Intel reported about $8.1 billion in sales for its CCPG segment, down 9% sequentially, according to its Oct. 29 earnings report and transcript — a "dramatic slowdown" primarily driven by depressed PC demand, the suit alleges.

Why Intel Stock Just Dropped

Pity Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) investors. Not only have they had to deal with the fallout of an Nvidia CEO scandal not of their making this month -- one that's contributed to an 18% drop in stock price in November alone.

Not only are they now struggling to parse a new SemiAnalysis report warning that capital spending on AI chips in 2027 could be 19% below previous estimates, 2028 spending might be 28% below, and 2029 spending could fall 41% below estimates.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Today, Intel investors are facing yet another negative catalyst for their stock. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), it seems, is selling down its stake in its semiconducting rival -- and it's costing Intel stock a 2.3% decline through 1:30 p.m. ET today.

Image source: Intel.

Nvidia cashes out

Nvidia just confirmed in an SEC filing that it has sold 25% of its Intel stock position, reducing its stake from 214.8 million shares to 161.1 million. At the same time, as StreetInsider.com reports, Nvidia has increased its ownership in SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) by 6%, to 130.5 million shares.

All of these numbers are as of Sept. 30, before the Jensen Huang scandal broke.

What's next for Intel

Nvidia's moves proved prescient. Although SpaceX stock has fallen slightly since the report date (down about 6%), Intel shares are down much, much more -- roughly 55%. So Nvidia kept a lot of its Intel profits by cashing out before Intel crashed (a crash that Nvidia's own CEO scandal helped cause).

The question for Intel investors now is: should you follow Nvidia's example and sell out of Intel, too? Before you do that, recall that if Nvidia sold 25% of its Intel shares in September, then it also kept 75%.

So Nvidia hasn't abandoned all hope in Intel yet. Maybe you shouldn't either?

Intel: a quarter of the stake sold

Nvidia bought its Intel shares in 2025, paying $5 billion, or $23.28 a share. On September 30 the remaining 161.1 million shares were worth $19.4 billion, about $120.23 a share. Nvidia has not said when it sold or at what price; a 13F shows only what a company held at the end of the quarter.

Intel has fallen hard since then. At 1:50 p.m. ET on Tuesday it was at $53.80, 55.3% below its September 30 value, which puts the stake Nvidia still held on that date at about $8.7 billion. title: Intel stock collapses; shareholders say they were misled
detail:
Intel stock collapses; shareholders say they were misled
Opeyemi Babalola, Celine Provini
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 11:47 AM CST 5 min read
INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Plenty of people priced a new laptop this year and decided the old one could hang on a little longer. A new lawsuit against Intel Corporation (INTC) argues that those small decisions piled up into a problem that the chipmaker kept from its own investors.

The proposed class action was filed on Nov. 13, 2026, by a pension fund for police and firefighters in Southfield, Michigan. It says PC makers and distributors were sitting on a "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory." Rising component prices had scared buyers off, the complaint says.

The fund's message is blunt. It says Intel, CEO Lip-Bu Tan, and CFO David Zinsner misled investors about how badly the PC slowdown was hurting the business. It also says Intel raised $23 billion from new shareholders in the middle of that quarter.

Also read: Intel CEO reveals a PC problem as Goldman cuts stock target

Intel's July report painted a calmer picture

The story begins on July 23, 2026, when Intel reported second-quarter results. Tan called it the company's strongest revenue growth in more than 15 years, according to the complaint.

On the call, Zinsner said the PC business was holding up, despite component shortages and rising prices, the suit says. He acknowledged that memory costs were straining the wider PC market. Still, he told analysts that Intel's own PC group would likely come in slightly higher in the third quarter.

Three weeks later, on Aug. 12, Intel sold more than 240 million new shares at $95 apiece, according to the complaint. Intel's earnings release describes the raise as funding to support future growth. Those shares later fell about 45% below the offering price, the complaint says.

A Michigan pension fund says Intel downplayed its PC slump before raising $23 billion in new stock, weeks ahead of a nearly 29% one-day plunge.hapabapa / Getty Images
The October report revealed a deeper PC slump

Intel's third-quarter report on Oct. 29 looked healthy at first glance. Total revenue rose 21% from a year earlier, according to Intel's earnings release. Data center and AI sales did the lifting, jumping 78%.

The trouble was in PCs. Revenue in that group fell 9% from the prior quarter, according to the complaint, instead of rising as Zinsner had suggested in July. That group brings in roughly half of Intel's revenue, based on the release, so the miss hurt.

The outlook was worse. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, according to the release. The complaint says that was about $1.5 billion below Wall Street's expectations.

Zinsner also said in the release that Intel sees the "PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year." By Intel's own forecast, no PC rebound comes before mid-2027.

Key Takeaways

Soros Fund Management's latest 13F shows its five biggest positions at Sept. 30 were Intel, Amazon, Taiwan Semiconductor, Alphabet and NVIDIA.

Among its positions of 2% or more, those five are also where Wall Street sees the most upside, with analysts' average targets 27% to 71% above the latest prices.

Four of the five have fallen sharply since Sept. 30 in a selloff in chip and AI stocks, which accounts for much of that upside.

Taiwan Semiconductor looks like the best buy of the five: its sales are still growing fast, and analysts kept raising its target through the selloff.

Few names in investing are as big as George Soros, so his firm's filings get read closely. Soros Fund Management's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 13, shows $6.48 billion of US stocks spread across 234 positions.

Its five biggest positions were all AI bets: three chip companies and two cloud giants. Among its positions of 2% or more, they're also the five where Wall Street sees the most upside, partly because four of them have fallen hard since Sept. 30. (Those moves are from each stock's Sept. 30 price, since a 13F doesn't show what the fund paid, or whether it still owns the shares.)

1. NVIDIA at 13x earnings, without Jensen Huang

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) was the fund's fifth-biggest position: 858,822 shares worth $196 million at Sept. 30, or 3.0% of the portfolio, after it cut the stake 19% in the quarter. It also held NVIDIA put options with a notional value of $80 million, which offset part of that bet. The stock has dropped 32% since, and on Nov. 12 Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, with CFO Colette Kress stepping in as interim CEO. The 62 analysts covering NVIDIA still see it reaching $268 on average, 71% above the last close. That target rose from $234 a year ago to a peak of $329 in late October before falling back:

NVIDIA (NVDA): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

At about 13x forward earnings, NVIDIA trades far below its five-year average of 36x. But its board is still looking for a permanent CEO, and the company reports its quarter this week.

2. Intel needs its estimates to stop falling

Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) was the fund's biggest position: 2.83 million shares worth $340 million, or 5.3% of the portfolio, after it grew the stake 2,730% in the third quarter. The stock has dropped 54% since Sept. 30, much of it after a weak fourth-quarter outlook on Oct. 29. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in Intel's third-quarter release that the immediate priority is "to unlock additional supply to meet extraordinary demand for our Xeon family." Since that report, analysts have cut their 2027 earnings estimate to $1.79 a share, from $2.11.
